CLASS 28 · PRESCHOOL AGES 4–5

Phonics & Beginning Sounds

Age 4–5 YearsClass 28 of 28Adventures 24 sound gamesSubjects Sounds · rhymes · words

Phonics is listening made visible: this class plays with the sounds inside words — first sounds, ending sounds, rhymes, syllables and the tiny vowels that hide in the middle. Twenty-four draw-on-the-picture adventures, each with a printable worksheet in the Phonics worksheet library.

Every game speaks: words and pure letter sounds play out loud, with replay and a mute switch. No reading required — ears lead, letters follow.

Meet the adventures ↓Grown-up nearby for the first round makes everything smoother.
TODAY’S CLASS

How this class works.

Phonics asks a new kind of listening: not what a word means, but what it is MADE of. The class walks up a gentle slope — hear a sound, find it in pictures, hear it at the start or end of words, blend sounds into words, swap sounds to make new words, and finally count the invisible sounds inside what you hear.

  1. 1 Warm-up: the first-sound games
  2. 2 Rhymes and blending
  3. 3 Two or three adventures from the shelves
  4. 4 The matching worksheet, printed
  5. 5 Class complete

TAKE IT OFF SCREEN

Sound play in the kitchen and the car.

I spy, with my little ear

  • “I spy something that starts with sss…” — soap, sock, spoon. Ears only, no letters needed.
  • Swap roles and let your child be the spy.

Stretched-word soup

  • Say a word stretched out — “mmmuuunnnch” — and let your child squash it back together.
  • Silly voices welcome; the stretching is the point.

Rhyme sandwiches

  • Any rhyme pair becomes a sandwich: “cat-hat sandwich, please!”
  • Make the order, serve it, giggle, repeat.

Phonics rewards tiny sessions. Five minutes of sound play, done warmly, beats thirty done tired.

A NOTE FROM THE PRINCIPAL

For the grown-ups.

Phonics has one famous rule: sounds first, letter names second. The letter is “em” but the sound is “mmm” — and children who learn the sound first learn to read with less un-learning. Every game here plays real recordings of both words and pure sounds; press replay as often as needed, and say the sounds with your child so the ears have company.

The printable worksheets are built to work without any audio: every sheet tells you exactly what to say and includes a grown-up answer line. Browse the phonics worksheets and print the twin of whichever game your child loved.

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Apple — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson opens the whole alphabet: the letter Aa and its first sound, the big open "ah" that starts apple. Your child traces the letter on the card, plays the doctor game that makes the sound naturally, and hunts A-sounds around the home.

What is this?

Aa is the letter that stands for the first sound in apple — a short, wide "ah". It is the first letter of the alphabet and the first sound on the path to reading.

What does it mean?

The big idea hiding in this lesson: a letter is a picture of a sound. When your child sees Aa and hears "ah" in their head, reading has officially started.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three things from this card: that Aa stands for the apple sound, that the sound is short and open (not the letter name "ay"), and that the sound can start many words, not only apple.

Why this matters

/a/ is one of the most common first sounds in little-word land — apple, ant, animal, am. A solid "ah" makes every later vowel lesson easier, because the mouth already knows how to open wide.

What it teaches

Wide-open mouth control (the biggest mouth-shape a vowel asks for), sound-to-letter mapping, and the listening habit of catching a sound at the start of a word.

Words to learn

aappleantapronalligatorah

Say this to your child

“"Open your mouth like the doctor asks — ahhh. That is the sound! A says ahh, like the start of apple. Say it with me and let your mouth open as wide as it can."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Aa. This is the letter. It says ah — ah — apple."
  2. Finger-trace the big Aa on the canvas while saying "ah" the whole way round — eyes, fingertip and voice on the same letter at once.
  3. Play the doctor game below: the sound arrives on its own, no drilling needed.
  4. Hunt three a-things in the room and name each one with a big open mouth: apple, animal, apron.
  5. Finish by letting your child say "ah — apple" all by themselves, and celebrate loudly.

How to say it

Drop the jaw, tongue flat and low, and let the voice out with nothing blocking it: "ah". No lip rounding, no teeth touching — the sound is pure open mouth.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Aa sits beside a shiny red apple with a single green leaf, and the word "apple" is printed underneath — letter, picture and word in one glance.

Ask your child

"What sound does A make?" "What is the picture word on this card?" "Can you find something that starts with ah?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "A says ah!" "Ah — apple!" or, mid-doctor-game, a very serious "ahhh" with the tongue out like a real check-up.

Out in the real world

The doctor game is the secret: every check-up ends with "say ahh" — and that IS the A sound. Add apple slices at snack time and ants on the pavement, and the sound has three homes already.

Try it together

Doctor check-up: wrap a scarf around your head, hold a spoon like a tongue depressor and ask your patient to "say ahh". After three "ahhhs", the doctor prescribes an a-word — apple, ant, apron. Swap roles and be the patient yourself.

Understanding check

Show the card again tomorrow and ask "what sound?" — a quick "ah!" (not "ay") means the sound has landed. If they give the letter name, replay the doctor game; the name can wait for the alphabet song.

Parent tips

The sound and the name are two different lessons. If "ay" keeps arriving, go back to the open-mouth game — the mouth remembers what the ears forget, and apples help.

This lesson pairs with the Apple flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

And when the lesson turns into snack time, the fruit itself has a card too: the Apple flashcard in Fruits & Vegetables — that one is for naming the fruit, this lesson is for the letter A.

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Ball — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Bb and its lip-pop sound with the ball card: your child traces the letter, blows up an imaginary balloon one b-word at a time, and learns that b is a sound they can feel on their own lips.

What is this?

Bb is the letter that stands for the first sound in ball — a quick pop made with two lips and a buzzing voice.

What does it mean?

B teaches that sounds live in the body, not just in the ear: /b/ happens on the lips, so your child can watch themselves say it in a mirror — a sound you can see is a sound you remember.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs to feel the lips press together before the pop, hear the voice buzzing behind the pop, and carry the sound onto other words — ball, bat, bubble — not just the picture word.

Why this matters

/b/ opens dozens of everyday words — ball, bath, book, breakfast, bus. It is also the twin of /p/, and children who feel the buzz-versus-puff difference early never mix the two spellings later.

What it teaches

Lip strength and control, voice awareness (feeling the throat buzz), and mirror self-checking — the first step toward fixing sounds without being told.

Words to learn

bballbatbubblebathbig

Say this to your child

“"Press your lips together like this — now hum until they pop open: buh. That is b! B says buh, like ball. Bounce the sound: buh, buh, ball."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Bb. Press your lips together — b! It says the ball sound."
  2. Finger-trace the tall Bb on the canvas while humming "b-b-b" — the tracing finger and the buzzing lips work together.
  3. Play the balloon game below so the sound gets a body to live in.
  4. Hunt b-things: a book, a bottle, a bear. Say each one with the same lip pop.
  5. End with the mirror check: lips together, voice on — "that is a real b!"

How to say it

Lips sealed, then released with the voice already running: "buh". The throat buzzes the whole time — a hand on the throat proves it. Keep the pop short; no "buh-uh" drag.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Bb sits beside a smiling beach ball in yellow, red and blue, with the word "ball" printed below — the toy most children already own, wearing its first letter.

Ask your child

"Where do your lips go for b?" "Does your throat buzz when you say it?" "What b-word should we bounce next?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "B! buh-buh-ball!" or — halfway through the balloon game — the classic complaint: "My lips are tired." Tired lips are learning lips.

Out in the real world

Ball games, bath time and bubble mix are three b-factories you already own. On walks, every bus, bench and bird is a b-spot waiting to be claimed out loud.

Try it together

The balloon game: mime blowing up a balloon — one b-word per breath, and the balloon grows bigger each time: ball… ball-bat… ball-bat-bubble. On the biggest word, let go: the balloon flies around the room with a long "bbbbbb" until it lands.

Understanding check

Ask for the sound, never the letter: "what sound does B make?" — a clean "buh" with lips visibly pressed is the goal. Then swap in a picture of a dog: if they say "nope, that is d", the sounds are sorted.

Parent tips

If b comes out as p, slow everything down and add the throat hand: b buzzes, p does not. Never drill longer than five minutes — the lips learn fast and sulk when tired.

This lesson pairs with the Ball flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Cat — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Cc and its click sound with the cat card: your child traces the letter, knocks on an imaginary castle door one c-word at a time, and discovers that the sound lives at the very back of the mouth.

What is this?

Cc is the letter that stands for the first sound in cat — a clean, short /k/ click made when the back of the tongue lets go of the roof of the mouth.

What does it mean?

C introduces a listening challenge: the click happens where no eye can see it. So this lesson teaches ears-first learning — the same skill every later sound lesson will reuse.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs to hear the click as a tiny door shutting, say it cleanly (no "kuh-uh" drag), and collect a small family of c-words — cat, cup, car — so the sound detaches from one picture.

Why this matters

/c/ is everywhere in a child’s day — cup, coat, car, cake, colour. It is also the first letter with a hidden second job (soft c, as in circus), and knowing the hard click first keeps that later surprise small.

What it teaches

Back-of-mouth tongue control, careful listening (the click is invisible), and word-family building — one sound, many words.

Words to learn

ccatcupcarcoatclick

Say this to your child

“"Knock knock — who is at the door? C! C says k, a tiny click like a door shutting: cat. Say it like a secret knock: c, c, cat."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Cc. It says the cat sound — a little click at the back: c!"
  2. Finger-trace the Cc on the canvas — the open curve matches the open back of the mouth.
  3. Play the castle-knock game below; the click IS the knock.
  4. Collect c-things: a cup, a carrot, a coat. Say each with one clean click.
  5. Finish with three fast clicks — c, c, cat — and a victory meow.

How to say it

Open the mouth slightly, lift the back of the tongue and let it drop: "k". Keep it dry and short — one click, no vowel hanging on. If "kuh-uh" appears, say it like a whisper-tick.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Cc sits beside a smiling orange tabby cat, with the word "cat" printed underneath — the most classic of all first phonics words.

Ask your child

"Can you feel the click at the back of your mouth?" "What did the cat say at the door?" "Name a c-word in this room."

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "c-c-c-cat!" with three knocks, or invent the best game of all: knocking on the actual table for every c-word they can find.

Out in the real world

The kitchen is a c-museum: cups, cabinets, carrots, cake tins. Car rides supply car, seat, clunk-click. And every story with a cat in it re-opens the door for one more knock.

Try it together

Castle knock: build a pillow fortress, and the only way in is the password — a c-word said with a proper click. Knock knock: "cat!" — the gate opens. Inside, the royal cat demands three more c-words before bed.

Understanding check

Ask "what sound does C make?" and listen for a clean click, not the letter name "see". Then test the family: cup, car, coat — three clicks in a row means the sound travels.

Parent tips

Do not mention soft c (circus, celery) yet — one job per card. And if c and k blur together, say honestly: "they are twins, same sound, two coats" — the honesty saves tears later.

This lesson pairs with the Cat flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Dog — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Dd and its tongue-tap sound with the dog card: your child traces the letter, plays doorbell with an imaginary front door, and feels exactly where the tongue lands for every d-word.

What is this?

Dd is the letter that stands for the first sound in dog — a quick tap of the tongue tip just behind the top teeth, with the voice switched on.

What does it mean?

D teaches that some sounds have an address: the tongue taps one exact spot, every time. Finding that spot is body knowledge — and body knowledge never fades.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs to feel the tap behind the teeth, keep the voice buzzing through it, and let d start a whole visitor list of words — dog, dad, duck, door.

Why this matters

/d/ starts the words that run a family’s day: dad, dinner, door, done. It is the voiced twin of /t/, and feeling the buzz difference now is cheaper than fixing the spelling confusion later.

What it teaches

Tongue-tip precision, voice-on/voice-off awareness, and the rhythm habit — one tap, one sound, one word.

Words to learn

ddogdadduckdoordrum

Say this to your child

“"Put your tongue behind your teeth and let it bounce once — duh. That is d! D says duh, like dog. Knock the sound: d, d, dog."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Dd. The tongue taps — d! It says the dog sound."
  2. Finger-trace the Dd on the canvas while tapping: one curve of the letter, one tap of the tongue.
  3. Play the doorbell game below — every visitor brings a d-word.
  4. Tap out three d-things you can see or pretend: dog, doll, doughnut.
  5. Finish with the drum finale: four fast taps, one loud "d-d-d-dog!"

How to say it

Tongue tip up to the ridge behind the top teeth, then release with the voice on: "duh". Quick and light — the tap is one frame long, not a held sound.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Dd sits beside a smiling golden puppy wearing a green collar, with the word "dog" printed below — the animal most children name first, now wearing its letter.

Ask your child

"Where does your tongue go for d?" "Does your voice buzz?" "Who should come to our door next — a duck or a doll?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "d-d-d-dog!" like a drumroll, or — best case — start answering every "knock knock" at home with a new d-word.

Out in the real world

Every front door in your life is a d-game now: knock, say a d-word, enter. Walks supply dogs (real ones bark along), dads, and delivery vans that go ding-dong.

Try it together

Doorbell game: draw a door on paper or use a real door. Each "ding-dong" means a visitor arrives — and the visitor must be a d-word: dog, duck, dad, dragon. Open the door, greet the visitor by name, close the door, ring again. Ten rings, ten visitors, zero boredom.

Understanding check

Tomorrow, ask "what sound does D make?" and watch the tongue: a visible tap behind the teeth with a buzzing throat is a pass. Then try "t" — if the tap stays but the buzz stops, both twins are learned.

Parent tips

If dog comes out as "tog", the voice switch is off — hand on the throat, exaggerate the buzz. Keep sessions short: the tongue is a muscle and learns best in little bursts.

This lesson pairs with the Dog flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Elephant — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Ee and its short "eh" sound with the elephant card: your child traces the letter, cracks imaginary eggs that hatch e-words, and learns the relaxed middle-mouth vowel the whole alphabet leans on.

What is this?

Ee is the letter that stands for the first sound in elephant — a short, relaxed "eh" made with the mouth half open and the tongue resting flat.

What does it mean?

E is the alphabet’s hardest worker: it appears in more words than almost any other letter. Meeting it as a sound (not just a letter name "ee") saves years of reading guesswork.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs to hear the short "eh" as its own sound — different from "ee" in tree and from "eye" — and say it in a handful of words: elephant, egg, elf.

Why this matters

Short /e/ sits inside bed, red, ten, get — words a four-year-old uses daily. It is also the vowel children confuse with short /i/ most often, so an early, well-modelled "eh" pays off for years.

What it teaches

Mid-mouth vowel control, sound isolation in long words (eh-le-phant), and the patience to let a long word start slowly.

Words to learn

eelephanteggelfelfelbow

Say this to your child

“"Relax your mouth — halfway open, nothing stretched: eh. That is E’s sound, the elephant one. Say it like a tiny echo: eh, eh, elephant."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Ee. It says eh — the elephant sound. Say it softly: eh."
  2. Finger-trace the Ee on the canvas — three straight arms, like the letter itself.
  3. Play the egg-crack game below: every crack hatches an e-word.
  4. Stretch the long word together: "eh — eh — eh-le-phant". The sound lives at the front.
  5. Finish with three soft "eh"s and one elephant stomp.

How to say it

Mouth half open, tongue flat and forward, voice on: "eh". The sound is short and dry — no glide into "ee". If it slides, bite an imaginary lemon and try again.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Ee sits beside a smiling grey elephant with the word "elephant" printed below in its own rounded box — a long, friendly word that starts with the shortest of sounds.

Ask your child

"What sound starts elephant?" "Is your mouth big open, half open or closed for eh?" "What hatches from an egg?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "eh-eh-elephant!" like a trumpet warming up, or announce breakfast facts: "eggs start with eh!" — which is exactly the point.

Out in the real world

Breakfast is an e-lesson: eggs, elbows on the table. Every elephant in every picture book gets one more "eh". And elbows, escalators and elevators all start with the same relaxed sound.

Try it together

Egg-crack game: tap an imaginary egg on the edge of an imaginary bowl — "eh, eh, CRACK!" — and something e-shaped hatches out: an elf, an elephant, an empty cup. Name the hatchling, crack the next egg. Whoever cracks the most eggs names the most e-things.

Understanding check

A day later, show the card and ask for the sound. "Eh!" is the goal; "ee" means the letter name crept in — replay the egg game, and keep your own "eh" short and flat so there is one model only.

Parent tips

Short /e/ and short /i/ mix up for years — that is normal, not failure. Model clearly, accept close attempts, and let many e-words do the sorting rather than corrections.

This lesson pairs with the Elephant flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Fish — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Ff and its windy sound with the fish card: your child traces the letter, powers a paper fan with f-breaths, and learns the one sound they can watch move a real object across a table.

What is this?

Ff is the letter that stands for the first sound in fish — air hissing gently between top teeth and bottom lip, with no voice at all.

What does it mean?

F is the first "quiet" sound in the set: the throat stays silent while the mouth makes wind. That contrast — voiced versus breath — is a listening skill the whole alphabet will reuse.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs the teeth-on-lip shape, the feel of moving air (not voice), and a small fleet of f-words — fish, frog, fork, fan — so the sound travels beyond one picture.

Why this matters

/f/ starts four, five, fish, family — words that organise a child’s whole day. It is also the whisper twin of /v/, and the hand-on-throat check learned here sorts both letters forever.

What it teaches

Lip-and-teeth coordination, air control (blowing gently on purpose), and voice-off awareness — noticing that some sounds run on breath alone.

Words to learn

ffishfrogforkfanfour

Say this to your child

“"Bite your bottom lip softly with your top teeth — now blow: fff. That is f! F says fff, like fish. Blow the sound: fff, fff, fish."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Ff. Top teeth kiss the bottom lip and blow — f! The fish sound."
  2. Finger-trace the Ff on the canvas: two arms and a leg, while the lips hold the wind.
  3. Play the paper-fan game below — the breath becomes visible and useful.
  4. Collect f-things: a fork, a feather, a picture of a frog. Say each with one soft gust.
  5. Finish with the mirror check: teeth visible on the lip means a true f.

How to say it

Top teeth rest lightly on the bottom lip, air pushes through, voice off: "fff". It can stretch as long as the breath lasts — the only limit is air.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Ff sits beside a smiling teal fish with the word "fish" printed below — a swims-along animal for a swims-along sound.

Ask your child

"Can you feel the wind on your lip?" "Is your throat quiet or buzzing?" "How long can your f last — three seconds? Five?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "fffish!" with a proper gust, or discover the party trick: f-ing at a candle flame and watching it bow.

Out in the real world

Fans, fridges and family dinners are f-territory. Feathers, falling leaves and foxes in storybooks all arrive pre-labelled with the sound — just say their names slowly.

Try it together

Paper-fan game: fold a paper fan (or use a real one), then power it with f-breaths only. Each gust must carry an f-word across the room: fish, frog, four. Race the fan against a feather — the breath that moves things is the right one.

Understanding check

Ask for the sound and watch the mouth: teeth on lip, moving air, silent throat. Then say v — if the buzz arrives and the shape stays, both twins are understood.

Parent tips

If fish becomes "vish", the voice snuck in — hand on the throat, no buzz on f. And keep the teeth soft: a gentle bite makes wind, a hard bite makes nothing.

This lesson pairs with the Fish flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Goat — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Gg and its growly sound with the goat card: your child traces the letter, plays the giggle game where laughing IS the sound, and feels /g/ buzzing right in the throat.

What is this?

Gg is the letter that stands for the first sound in goat — the back of the tongue lifts deep in the mouth and lets go with the voice growling.

What does it mean?

G teaches that sounds have homes: /g/ lives at the very back, the deepest spot in the mouth. Children feel it in the throat, and body-deep sounds stick for good.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs the throat-growl feel, a clean "guh" (no stretched "guh-uh"), and a few g-words beyond goat — go, gum, giggle — to prove the sound is theirs.

Why this matters

/g/ drives go, get, game, giggle — the action words of a four-year-old. It is also the twin of /k/ (same spot, g buzzes, k does not) and grows up into a second soft job later; the hard growl comes first.

What it teaches

Back-of-tongue control (the same spot as k, now with voice), throat awareness, and playful volume control — growls can be big or tiny.

Words to learn

ggoatgogumgigglegarden

Say this to your child

“"Put your hand on your throat. Now growl like a tiny goat: guh, guh. Feel it shake? That is g! G says guh, like goat."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Gg. It says g — a growl from way down: guh. The goat sound!"
  2. Finger-trace the Gg on the canvas — the circle and the hook — while growling softly.
  3. Play the giggle game below; laughing is rehearsal for g.
  4. Growl three g-things: goat, gum, gate. Hand on the throat to feel the buzz.
  5. Finish with one enormous silly goat growl — noise allowed.

How to say it

Back of the tongue lifts high and deep, then drops with the voice on: "guh". One drop, one sound — if it drags into "guh-uh", snap it shorter.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Gg sits beside a smiling white goat with little horns, and the word "goat" is printed below — the set’s comedians, wearing the growliest letter.

Ask your child

"Where do you feel g — lips, tongue or throat?" "Does it buzz?" "Growl me a g-word."

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "g-g-g-goat!" like a machine starting, or go straight for the joke: "giggle starts with g — g-g-giggle!" while collapsing into one.

Out in the real world

Gardens, gates and gum all grow g-words on demand. A farm visit or a goat video supplies the animal itself; giggling supplies the sound — free, unlimited, and already loved.

Try it together

Giggle game: the grown-up tries — really tries — NOT to laugh while saying g-words: goat, gum, gate. The child’s job is to make it impossible: silly faces, goat noises, fake sneezes. Every giggle that escapes must be named: "that was a g-giggle!"

Understanding check

Ask "what sound does G make?" and listen for the growl, not "jee". Then try k — same spot, no buzz. If the throat sorts them apart, both letters are learning-proof.

Parent tips

If g and k swap, the throat hand is the referee: g buzzes, k stays quiet. And skip soft g (giraffe) for now — the goat owns this card; giraffes can visit another year.

This lesson pairs with the Goat flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Hat — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Hh and its breath sound with the hat card: your child traces the letter, fogs a mirror (or a window) with h-breaths, and learns the quietest letter in the whole set.

What is this?

Hh is the letter that stands for the first sound in hat — a soft puff of air, no mouth shape, no voice: just breath with a letter on it.

What does it mean?

H is the alphabet’s whisper: it proves that some sounds are almost nothing at all. Learning to hear almost-nothing is real listening training — the hardest listening there is.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs to feel the h-puff on their own hand, hear the difference between "hat" and "at" (one breath changes everything), and keep the puff gentle.

Why this matters

/h/ starts hand, help, home, hungry — words a child says every single day. It is also the sound children most often drop ("at" for hat), and playful breath games bring it back without a single correction.

What it teaches

Breath control, gentle air awareness, and the fine listening that separates a puff from silence.

Words to learn

hhathandhousehothello

Say this to your child

“"Breathe out warm air on your hands, like fogging a window: hhh. That is h! H says hhh, like hat. Warm your hands with the sound."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Hh. It is only breath — hhh, like warming your hands. The hat sound!"
  2. Finger-trace the Hh on the canvas: two tall posts and a bridge, while huffing softly.
  3. Play the mirror-fog game below — the breath becomes something you can see.
  4. Huff three h-things: hat, hand, house. Small puffs, clear words.
  5. Finish by whispering "hat" without the h, then with it — hear the magic puff arrive.

How to say it

Open the mouth slightly and sigh warm air: "hhh". No voice, no shape, no effort — the laziest sound in English. If it becomes "kuh", the throat woke up; relax it again.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Hh sits beside a blue fedora hat with a red band, and the word "hat" is printed below — the letter that is barely a sound, on the card that is easy to wear.

Ask your child

"Can you feel the warm air?" "Is h loud or quiet?" "Say hat — now say at. What changed?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "hhhhat!" with a proper fog-cloud, or invent the game nobody taught: huffing at every window in the house and drawing h-letters in the fog.

Out in the real world

Bath steam, cold-morning breath and hot soup all make real h-clouds. Story wolves huff famously. And every hello, hat and hand is one puff away from practice.

Try it together

Mirror-fog game: hold a hand mirror (or use any window) and fog it with h-breaths. Before the fog fades, draw a big H in it with a fingertip and name an h-word — hat, hand, house. Fog, draw, name; fog, draw, name. The window does the scoring.

Understanding check

Show the card tomorrow and ask for the sound: a soft, visible breath is the pass. Then say "at" and "hat" back to back — if your child hears the difference, the dropped-h habit is already curing itself.

Parent tips

Never chase the dropped h with corrections — huff the breath first, then add the word, and the h returns on its own. Whispering h on purpose also works: quiet sounds make children listen harder.

This lesson pairs with the Hat flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Igloo — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Ii and its quick "ih" sound with the igloo card: your child traces the letter, plays the itch game that pulls the sound out naturally, and meets the smallest, quickest vowel in the alphabet.

What is this?

Ii is the letter that stands for the first sound in igloo — a short, tight "ih" made with the mouth barely open and the tongue high and forward.

What does it mean?

I proves that vowels come in sizes: /a/ is a wide-open house, /i/ is a tiny snow hut. The mouth barely moves, the sound barely lasts — and it is still a whole letter.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs to hear the quick "ih" as different from "eye" (the letter name) and from "ee", and to say it inside little words: igloo, in, insect, it.

Why this matters

Short /i/ runs the small words that hold sentences together — it, in, is, big, him. A child who owns "ih" can soon read the glue-words that make sentences stick.

What it teaches

Tiny-movement vowel control (the opposite skill of wide-open a), quick sound production, and listening for small differences between close vowels.

Words to learn

iiglooininsectitinch

Say this to your child

“"Make your mouth tiny — barely open: ih. That is I’s sound, the igloo one. Say it quick like a tickle: ih, ih, igloo."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Ii. It says ih — quick and small, like the start of igloo."
  2. Finger-trace the Ii on the canvas: one tall stick and a dot — the shortest letter-shape, the shortest sound.
  3. Play the itch game below; "ih" arrives with the scratching.
  4. Say three tiny i-words together: in, it, insect. Keep the sound quick.
  5. Finish with the inch test: move one small inch across the floor per i-word.

How to say it

Mouth barely open, tongue high and forward, one quick beat: "ih". It is the shortest vowel — over and fast. If it stretches into "ee", tighten everything and try again.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Ii sits beside a snowy ice igloo with a round doorway, and the word "igloo" is printed below — a house built from the same stuff as the sound: small, quick, cool.

Ask your child

"Is your mouth big or tiny for ih?" "What is the picture on the card?" "Can you say three little i-words?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "ih-ih-igloo!" with tiny nibbling mouth moves, or report honestly: "insect starts with ih — I have one in my tummy." Both count.

Out in the real world

Insects in the garden, ink on fingertips, itchy jumpers — "ih" hides in daily life. Inside-and-on top of that: every "in", "it" and "is" your child hears all day is a secret i-drill.

Try it together

Itch game: pretend something is itchy — an arm, a nose, a knee. Scratch and announce: "ih — itchy!" Then scratch-itch other things and name them: an itchy insect, an itchy igloo, an itchy inchworm. Whoever scratches the silliest body part wins the round.

Understanding check

Show the card the next day and ask for the sound: a quick "ih" (not "eye", not "ee") is the pass. Then hide the card and say "igloo" — if the first sound arrives tight and fast, the vowel is owned.

Parent tips

Short /i/ and long /i/ (ice, eye) are different jobs — keep this card’s sound tiny and quick. If "eegloo" keeps coming, whisper it: quiet forces the mouth small.

This lesson pairs with the Igloo flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Jam — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Jj and its jumping sound with the jam card: your child traces the letter, wobbles like jelly through a j-word game, and feels the tongue jump that every j-word starts with.

What is this?

Jj is the letter that stands for the first sound in jam — the tongue starts behind the teeth and jumps forward with the voice buzzing: j-j-jam.

What does it mean?

J is a movement sound: it does not sit still like m or s, it jumps. Children who learn j as motion — jump, jiggle, jog — are learning the sound and the action at once.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs the quick tongue jump with voice on, a clean "juh", and a jar-full of j-words: jam, jump, juice, jog.

Why this matters

/j/ opens jump, joy, jam and jacket — the energy words of childhood. It is also the twin of /ch/ (same spot, j buzzes, ch puffs), a distinction worth feeling early.

What it teaches

Front-tongue jump control, voice awareness, and syllable play — j-words tend to be bouncy, and bouncy words are rhythm practice in disguise.

Words to learn

jjamjumpjuicejogjelly

Say this to your child

“"Put your tongue up, then let it jump out: juh. That is j! J says juh, like jam. Jump the sound: j, j, jam."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Jj. The tongue jumps — j! It says the jam sound."
  2. Finger-trace the Jj on the canvas: the hook jumps down below the line, like the tongue jumping forward.
  3. Play the jelly-wobble game below — every j-word wobbles.
  4. Jump-say three j-things: jam, jump, juice. One small jump each.
  5. Finish with a whole-body jelly wobble and a loud "j-j-jam!"

How to say it

Tongue tip starts behind the top teeth and springs forward with the voice buzzing: "juh". Quick and springy — one jump, no slide into "zh".

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Jj sits beside a strawberry jam jar with a red gingham lid, and the word "jam" is printed below — the stickiest card on the shelf, for the springiest sound.

Ask your child

"Does your tongue jump or sit still for j?" "Is your throat buzzing?" "What j-word makes you wobble best?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "j-j-jam!" with real jumps, or make the breakfast connection unprompted: "juice starts with j — pour the j-sound!"

Out in the real world

Jam, juice and jelly live at the breakfast table; jumps and jiggles live everywhere. Jackets, jeans and jigsaws fill the rest of the day — every one a j-word asking to be said slowly.

Try it together

Jelly-wobble game: whenever anyone says a j-word, everyone wobbles like a plate of jelly — jam! wobble. jump! wobble. jog! wobble. The grown-up’s job is to say j-words fast; the child’s job is to keep wobbling without falling over. Falling over is, of course, a j too: j-just get back up.

Understanding check

Ask for the sound tomorrow: a springy "juh" with a buzzing throat is the pass. Then try ch — same spot in the mouth, puff instead of buzz. If the swap lands, the tongue has learned two letters for the price of one.

Parent tips

If j drifts to a y-sound, slow the jump down and exaggerate it. And keep it English-juh: in some languages j whispers differently — this card teaches the jumping English j.

This lesson pairs with the Jam flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Kite — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Kk and its click sound with the kite card: your child traces the letter, turns imaginary keys that unlock k-words, and learns the big spelling secret that two letters can share one sound.

What is this?

Kk is the letter that stands for the first sound in kite — the very same back-of-the-mouth click that c makes in cat, here in its own shape.

What does it mean?

K is the alphabet’s spelling lesson in disguise: the click your child already owns now has a second written home. Meeting it as a fun fact — never a test — keeps both spellings friendly for life.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs to recognise the click as the same one c makes, say it cleanly for k-words — kite, kick, key — and feel proud rather than confused about the two coats.

Why this matters

/k/ keeps kick, key, kitchen and kind running. Meeting it as "c’s twin" early prevents the classic later tear: "but why does cat start with c and kite with k?"

What it teaches

Back-click control (second visit), sound identity beyond letter shapes, and the flexible thinking that lets one sound belong to two letters.

Words to learn

kkitekickkeykingkiss

Say this to your child

“"Here is a secret: K and C make the very same click. K just wears its own coat. Say it: k, k, kite — the wind sound!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Kk. It says k — the same click as cat, in a new coat: kite!"
  2. Finger-trace the Kk on the canvas: one tall post, one arm and one leg — a letter built like a little person.
  3. Play the key-turn game below; every turn unlocks a k-word.
  4. Click three k-things: kite, king, keys. Listen for the same click as cat.
  5. Finish by saying cat, then kite — and announcing: "same sound, two letters!"

How to say it

Identical to hard c: back of the tongue lifts and releases, voice off: "k". One dry click, no vowel trailing.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Kk sits beside a colourful diamond kite with two bows on its tail, and the word "kite" is printed below — the flying toy that owns the second click-spelling.

Ask your child

"What sound does K make?" "Is it the same sound as cat?" "What k-word should we unlock next?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "k-k-k-kite!" with three tugs, or deliver the lesson better than any adult: "c and k are twins!" — a fact they will repeat to everyone.

Out in the real world

Keys at every door, kicks in every garden, kings in every storybook. Windy days are kite days; windy days are also k-practice days.

Try it together

Key-turn game: mime holding a giant ring of keys. Each turn — click! — must unlock a k-word before the imaginary door opens: kite, king, kiss, kitchen. Open the door, peek inside, close it, pick the next key. Ten keys, ten words, one very heavy ring.

Understanding check

Ask "what sound does K make?" — the goal is the click AND the twin-fact: "same as c!" Then hide the card and ask for kite, kick, key in a row; three clean clicks mean the second coat fits.

Parent tips

Do not make the c/k difference a problem — it is a fun fact, not a quiz. Say "twins with two coats" once, play the keys, and let the spelling sort itself out years later.

This lesson pairs with the Kite flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Lion — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Ll and its singing sound with the lion card: your child traces the letter, climbs an imaginary ladder one l-word per rung, and keeps the tongue tip up — the whole secret of l.

What is this?

Ll is the letter that stands for the first sound in lion — the tongue tip lifts behind the top teeth and the voice sings around its sides: l-l-lion.

What does it mean?

L shows that consonants can be vowels’ warm-up acts: the voice flows AROUND the sides of the lifted tongue instead of stopping. That side-flow is why l blends so smoothly into the vowels that follow it.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs the tongue-tip-up feel, the singing hold, and a pride of l-words — lion, leg, love, lullaby — spoken with the tip visibly lifting.

Why this matters

/l/ starts look, love, like and lunch — the warmest words in a small child’s day. It is also one of the last sounds to mature, so gentle games now beat corrections later.

What it teaches

Tongue-tip lift and hold, sustained voicing (singing a consonant), and mirror self-checking — with l, the tongue tip is visible when done right.

Words to learn

llionlegliplovelullaby

Say this to your child

“"Put your tongue tip up behind your teeth and let it sing: llll. That is l! L says lll, like lion. Climb the sound: l, l, lion."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Ll. The tongue tip goes up and sings — l! The lion sound."
  2. Finger-trace the Ll on the canvas: one tall post and one foot — the same shape as a tongue tip lifting, say it while you draw it.
  3. Play the ladder-climb game below — one rung, one l-word.
  4. Sing three l-things: lion, leg, love. Hold each l as long as breath allows.
  5. Finish with the mirror check: tongue tip visible at the top teeth means a true l.

How to say it

Tongue tip pressed lightly behind the top teeth, voice on, air flowing around the sides: "lll". It holds — sing it long. If it turns into "w" ("yion"), the tip is not lifting.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Ll sits beside a golden lion with a great dark mane, and the word "lion" is printed below — and the mane curls exactly like a lowercase l, a shape-lesson hiding in the picture.

Ask your child

"Can you see your tongue tip?" "How long can your l sing?" "What l-word should we climb to next?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "lllllion!" with a five-second hold, or point at the mane and shout the shape-fact: "the lion has little l’s all over his head!"

Out in the real world

Ladders, lifts and legs; lips, lamps and love. The zoo lion roars once and the lullaby sings it again at bedtime — the sound is everywhere a child is.

Try it together

Ladder-climb game: stand tall and climb an invisible ladder, one rung per l-word — leg, lip, log, lift. Each climb ends on a shelf where an l-thing waits to be named. Climb high enough and the top shelf holds the grand prize: a lion (soft toy recommended, roaring optional).

Understanding check

Ask for the sound and watch the mirror: a visible tongue tip with a singing hold is the pass. If l arrives as w, slow down, exaggerate the tip lift, and let the mirror do the correcting — no words needed.

Parent tips

/l/ is a late bloomer — "yion" is a stage, not a fault. Keep the games silly, keep the tip visible, and never practice longer than the giggles last.

This lesson pairs with the Lion flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Moon — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Mm and its humming sound with the moon card: your child traces the letter, hums the tasty hum before every pretend snack, and meets the sound their mouth has known since babyhood.

What is this?

Mm is the letter that stands for the first sound in moon — lips pressed together, voice humming straight through them: mmm.

What does it mean?

M is the sound children make before words: "mmm" for tasty, for thinking, for calling mum. Learning m is not learning something new — it is naming something already owned.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs the closed-lip hum, the feel of the buzz on the lips, and a moonful of m-words — moon, mum, milk, more — hummed into full words.

Why this matters

/m/ opens mum, milk, mine and more — the first-word family of almost every child. It is also the twin of /n/ (lips versus tongue tip), a difference the pinch-test makes loud and funny.

What it teaches

Closed-lip humming, voice awareness through the nose-versus-lips contrast, and connecting an owned sound to its written letter.

Words to learn

mmoonmummilkmoremmm

Say this to your child

“"Close your lips and sing through them: mmmm. That is m! M says mmm, like moon — and like the sound you make when dinner is delicious."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Mm. Close your lips and hum — mmm. The moon sound!"
  2. Finger-trace the Mm on the canvas: four little mountain legs, humming the whole way across.
  3. Play the tasty-hum game below — the hum becomes a meal.
  4. Hum-say three m-things: moon, milk, muffin. Lips closed until the vowel.
  5. Finish with the longest hum of the day, landed softly on "moon".

How to say it

Lips fully closed, voice humming through the nose and lips: "mmm". Hold it long, then open into the word — mmm-moon. If the lips part early, the m disappears; keep them sealed.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Mm sits beside a smiling full moon with soft craters, and the word "moon" is printed below — the night-sky friend for the sound children hum at bedtime anyway.

Ask your child

"Are your lips open or closed for m?" "Can you hum with your mouth shut?" "What m-word would you eat right now?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "mmmmoon!" with closed lips then a big open finish, or rate your cooking honestly: "mmm! that means m-words are coming."

Out in the real world

Mealtimes are m-festivals: mmm before every bite of mash, melon, muffin. Bedtime adds the moon itself, plus lullabies hummed on m — the sound already lives in your child’s favourite moments.

Try it together

Tasty-hum game: lay out pretend snacks (real ones work too). Before tasting each one, the eater must hum approval — "mmm!" — then name it with the hum attached: mmm-melon, mmm-muffin. Swap chef and critic roles. The tastiest-sounding m-word wins the last bite.

Understanding check

Show the card tomorrow and ask for the sound: a closed-lip hum is an instant pass — it is the hardest sound to get wrong. Then try n, and pinch the nose mid-hum: the buzz stops. M and n, sorted by nose.

Parent tips

If m-words start losing their front sound ("oon" for moon), hum the m and keep the lips closed until the last possible moment. The lips re-learn in one game.

This lesson pairs with the Moon flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Nest — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Nn and its nose-hum sound with the nest card: your child traces the letter, switches on pretend stars one n-word at a time, and learns how the nose joins the alphabet.

What is this?

Nn is the letter that stands for the first sound in nest — a quick tap of the tongue that turns into a hum, the sound a bottle makes as it empties: nnn.

What does it mean?

N shares one doorway with m: the nose. The only thing that changes is the tongue — resting at the lips for m, lifted behind the teeth for n. One body, two sounds, one fingertip apart.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs the tongue-tip-up hum, the nose-buzz feel (pinch test!), and a nest-full of n-words: nest, nose, night, nine.

Why this matters

/n/ carries no, night, nine and napkin — words with real power in a child’s day. It is also m’s twin, and sorting the two by tongue spot now prevents years of m/n spelling swaps.

What it teaches

Tongue-tip precision while humming, nose-versus-lips discrimination, and the fine mouth-awareness that separates close twin sounds.

Words to learn

nnestnosenightninenap

Say this to your child

“"Tap your tongue behind your teeth and hum — nnn. That is n! N says nnn, like nest. Feel it buzzing in your nose? N, n, nest."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Nn. Tongue tip up, hum through your nose — nnn. The nest sound!"
  2. Finger-trace the Nn on the canvas: two posts and a bridge, one nnn-hum per stroke.
  3. Play the night-stars game below — every n-word lights a star.
  4. Hum three n-things: nest, nose, night. Tongue tip stays high.
  5. Finish with the pinch test: hum n, pinch the nose, feel the buzz stop. Magic.

How to say it

Tongue tip pressed behind the top teeth, voice humming through the nose, mouth lightly closed or open: "nnn". The lips stay apart — if they close, you made an m.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Nn sits beside a brown nest holding three pale eggs, and the word "nest" is printed below — three eggs, free counting practice, riding on the sound.

Ask your child

"Where is your tongue for n?" "What happens if I pinch your nose while you hum?" "Name an n-word in this room."

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "nnnest!" with the nose-scrunch of a proper hum, or demand the pinch test on repeat — the buzz-stop is preschool comedy gold.

Out in the real world

Night-time is n-time: night, no, nose-wipe, nine bedtime hugs. Birds’ nests on walks, napkins at dinner, and the word no (said by both parties) keep the sound in rotation.

Try it together

Night-stars game: the room goes to night-time (lights can stay on; pretend dark is better). Each n-word said switches on one imaginary star: night… nose… nine… nest. Fill the whole ceiling, then count the stars — nine is, naturally, the best answer.

Understanding check

Ask for the sound and watch the tongue: tip up, nose buzzing. Then the referee game: m and n back to back — lips for m, tongue for n. If your child can show both, the twins are sorted.

Parent tips

Swap hunts work better than corrections here: say nest, nose and name in a row and let your child point to their nose or their lips each time they hear where the hum sits. The pointing finger learns faster than the correcting mouth — and no inside the nest stays the best n-word of all.

This lesson pairs with the Nest flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Octopus — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Oo and its round sound with the octopus card: your child traces the letter, plays the surprise-box game where every opening is an "O!", and learns the one letter that is also a perfect mouth shape.

What is this?

Oo is the letter that stands for the first sound in octopus — a short, round "oh" made with the lips curled into a little circle.

What does it mean?

O is the alphabet’s self-portrait: the letter looks like the mouth shape it needs. Show the letter, make the mouth — the shape teaches itself, which is why o is a favourite first vowel.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs the round-lip "oh", kept short (this is octopus /o/, not open /oh/), and a basket of o-words: octopus, on, off, ox.

Why this matters

/o/ powers on, off, hot, not, stop — the words that run a four-year-old’s day, including the most powerful one: stop. Short and round, and sentences start working.

What it teaches

Lip rounding control, letter-shape to mouth-shape mapping, and keeping a vowel short when the letter name wants to stretch it.

Words to learn

ooctopusonoffoxhot

Say this to your child

“"Make your lips into a little circle — oh! That is O’s sound, the octopus one. Say it round: oh, oh, octopus."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Oo. Round your mouth like this letter: oh! The octopus sound."
  2. Finger-trace the Oo on the canvas — a perfect circle, drawn while the lips hold their own perfect circle.
  3. Play the surprise-box game below; every lid-lift is a natural O.
  4. Round-say three o-things: on, off, octopus. Keep the sound short and round.
  5. Finish with eight arm-wiggles — one per arm, one per o-word.

How to say it

Lips rounded into a small circle, voice on, sound kept short: "oh". No glide up into "oh-uh" — clip it clean. The letter draws the mouth; the mouth draws the sound.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Oo sits beside a smiling purple octopus with curling arms, and the word "octopus" is printed below — eight arms for eight practice rounds, all starting with the same round sound.

Ask your child

"Is your mouth round or flat for o?" "What does the letter look like?" "Say on — now off. Both start with...?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "o-o-o-octopus!" with lips like a goldfish, or connect the shape forever: "O looks like my mouth when I say it!"

Out in the real world

On-and-off switches are o-controllers disguised as furniture. Hot and not, stop and go, octopuses in the bath — the round sound runs the day’s biggest moments.

Try it together

Surprise-box game: fill an imaginary box (or a real one) with mystery objects. Open the lid — "O!" — then name what is inside, starting with the sound you just made: an octopus, an orange, an ox. Close, shake, reopen. The louder the O, the bigger the surprise.

Understanding check

Show the card tomorrow and ask for the sound: a short round "oh" is the pass; a stretched "oh-ohh" means the long O visited — clip it short and move on. The surprise-box reopen is the quickest repair.

Parent tips

Short /o/ (octopus, on) and long /o/ (open, over) are different jobs. Keep this one round and clipped — the long O has its own cards elsewhere on the path.

This lesson pairs with the Octopus flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Pig — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Pp and its puff sound with the pig card: your child traces the letter, pops like corn on every p-word, and catches the invisible puff of air that separates p from its loud twin b.

What is this?

Pp is the letter that stands for the first sound in pig — lips pressed together, then a little burst of air with no voice: p-p-pig.

What does it mean?

P is invisible — nothing wiggles in the mouth to show it happened. So this lesson teaches the tissue trick and the mirror check: children learn to catch sounds they cannot see.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs the soft lip burst, the silent throat (p does not buzz), and a pen of p-words: pig, pop, park, pink.

Why this matters

/p/ runs please, play, park and popcorn — the polite-and-playful heart of a child’s day. It is also b’s twin, and the puff test learned here keeps the two spellings apart forever.

What it teaches

Lip-burst control, voice-off awareness (the b/p contrast), and instrument-based self-checking — tissue and mirror as the child’s own measuring tools.

Words to learn

ppigpopparkpinkpopcorn

Say this to your child

“"Press your lips together and let a tiny puff out: p! That is P’s sound, the pig one. Pop the sound: p, p, pig."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Pp. Lips together, little puff — p! The pig sound."
  2. Finger-trace the Pp on the canvas: one tall post and one round belly, puffing with each curve.
  3. Play the popcorn game below — every pop is a p-word.
  4. Puff-say three p-things: pig, pink, park. Throat silent, lips busy.
  5. Finish with the tissue test: p moves the tissue, b does not. Science!

How to say it

Lips sealed, then opened with a small air burst and no voice: "puh". Keep the puff small and quick — a big dramatic blast is fine for learning, quiet for talking.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Pp sits beside a smiling pink pig, and the word "pig" is printed below — the snout-nosed teacher for the sound with no voice and plenty of puff.

Ask your child

"Does your throat buzz for p?" "What happens to a tissue when you say p?" "What p-word would you plant in the garden?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "p-p-p-pig!" with popcorn jumps, or run the tissue experiment on the whole family — p, b, f, everything gets tested.

Out in the real world

Parks, picnics and puddles; pigs at the farm, penguins at the zoo. Popcorn nights put the sound right in the bowl — pop is the best p-word ever invented.

Try it together

Popcorn game: everyone crouches low like a seed in the pan. The grown-up pretends to pour oil, shake the pan and turn up the heat — and when the heat is HOT, each child pops up with a p-word: pop! pink! pig! park! Pop, say the word, sink back down, wait for the next shake. The biggest pop wins the pan.

Understanding check

Ask for the sound and hold the tissue: a visible jump with a silent throat is the pass. Then say b — same lips, buzzing, tissue still. If your child can feel both twins, p is fully learned.

Parent tips

If pig comes out as big, the voice switched on — hand on the throat proves p stays quiet. Exaggerate the puff while learning; the small everyday p arrives on its own.

This lesson pairs with the Pig flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Queen — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Qq, the only letter that carries two sounds at once: a /k/ click straight into a /w/ puff. Your child traces the letter, plays the quick-flash game, and learns why q never walks alone.

What is this?

Qq stands for the first sound in queen — /kw/, two sounds glued into one burst: the k click of cat followed instantly by the w of wind.

What does it mean?

Q is the set’s first two-sound letter — proof that letters can be teams. And q has a famous friend: almost every q in English brings the letter u, because u helps make the w.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs to feel the click-then-puff as ONE motion, hear /kw/ at the start of queen, quick and quiet, and know that q and u are a package deal.

Why this matters

/kw/ is rare but mighty: queen, quick, quilt and quiet are story-time royalty. Learning the two-in-one burst now makes the strangest letter feel like a trick, not a problem.

What it teaches

Sound blending at its smallest (two sounds, one burst), back-click plus lip-round coordination, and letter-team awareness (q + u forever).

Words to learn

qqueenquickquietquiltquack

Say this to your child

“"Make the k click and blow it into a puff of wind — kwuh! That is Q’s sound: two sounds in one. Say it royal: kw, kw, queen."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Qq. It says kw — a click and a puff in one: queen!"
  2. Finger-trace the Qq on the canvas: the circle, then the tail — and draw the u next to it, because q never travels alone.
  3. Play the quick-flash game below; every flash ends with a /kw/ word.
  4. Burst-say three q-things: queen, quick, quack. One click-puff each.
  5. Finish with a royal bow and a very quiet "quiet" — the hardest q-word, said perfectly.

How to say it

Back click (/k/) released straight into rounded lips (/w/), voice on: "kwuh". Said fast it is one burst; said slow it falls apart. Speed is the glue.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Qq sits beside a smiling queen with a golden crown and a purple gown, and the word "queen" is printed below — the majesty that owns the two-sound letter.

Ask your child

"How many sounds does q make?" "What letter always comes after q?" "Can you say quick as fast as possible?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "kw-kw-kween!" with royal waving, or spot the pattern forever after: "that word has q — where is its friend u?"

Out in the real world

Queens and quacks rule story-time; quilts wait at grandparents’ houses. Quick and quiet run every game of hide-and-seek — two q-words hiding in plain sight.

Try it together

Quick-flash game: the grown-up calls an action, the child does it QUICKLY — and announces each one with the /kw/ burst: clap kw-ickly! touch toes kw-ickly! sit down kw-ickly! Finish the round with the hardest command of all: "now be kw-iet" — a royal whisper wins the crown.

Understanding check

Ask what sound q makes and listen for the glue: "kw" as one burst (not "k…wuh" in two pieces) is the pass. Then ask what comes after q in a word — "u!" means the team-fact landed too.

Parent tips

Say /kw/ as one burst, not two separate sounds — slow it down only to demonstrate, then speed it back up. And enjoy the oddness: q is the weird one, and children love being insiders on the weird one.

This lesson pairs with the Queen flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Rabbit — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Rr and its curling sound with the rabbit card: your child traces the letter, revs like a race car, and learns the sound made where no mirror can see — pure listening, pure tongue.

What is this?

Rr is the letter that stands for the first sound in rabbit — the tongue curls up toward the roof of the mouth and touches NOTHING, while the voice runs: r-r-rabbit.

What does it mean?

R is the alphabet’s invisible one: no lips to watch, no tongue tip to see. Children who learn r by feel (the growl, the engine) beat children who learn it by instruction.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs the curled-tongue feel without touching, the running voice, and a warren of r-words: rabbit, run, red, rain.

Why this matters

/r/ drives run, red, ride and ready — the movement words of childhood. It is also famously the LAST sound to mature, so early playful exposure plants it without pressure.

What it teaches

Tongue-body control without visual feedback, sustained voicing, and trusting listening over looking — the deepest mouth-awareness lesson in the set.

Words to learn

rrabbitrunredrainroad

Say this to your child

“"Curl your tongue up like a wave and let the engine run: rrrr. That is r! R says rrr, like rabbit. Rev the sound: r, r, rabbit."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Rr. Curl your tongue up — but touch nothing! It says the rabbit sound."
  2. Finger-trace the Rr on the canvas: the tall post with its little arm — the arm curls, the tongue curls.
  3. Play the race-engine game below; the engine rev is the sound’s natural home.
  4. Run-say three r-things: rabbit, rain, red. Tongue curled, voice driving.
  5. Finish with three bunny hops, one r-word per hop.

How to say it

Tongue curled toward the roof of the mouth, close but touching nothing, voice on: "rrr". It can run like an engine. If it becomes w ("wabbit"), the tongue flattened — curl it again.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Rr sits beside a grey rabbit with long ears, and the word "rabbit" is printed below — the hoppiest animal in the set, carrying the sound children master last.

Ask your child

"Can your tongue touch anything for r?" "What does a race car say?" "What r-word hops?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "r-r-r-rabbit!" with full engine sounds, or request the growl game daily — revving is practice disguised as fun.

Out in the real world

Car rides are r-practice: roads, roundabouts, red lights, rain. Rabbit visits in storybooks, and every run around the garden is a chance to say run while doing it.

Try it together

Race-engine game: be the driver and the car. Start the engine — "rrr, rrr, rrrr" — then drive to a destination called out by the grown-up: a red cushion, a round table, the rabbit’s burrow. Park, turn the engine off, pick a new r-destination. Traffic noises encouraged; r-words required at every red light.

Understanding check

Ask for the sound: a running "rrr" with the tongue clearly NOT touching is the pass. If "wabbit" appears, stay calm — r is the last sound to settle, and growls and engines do the teaching without any corrections.

Parent tips

Skip the corrections entirely — “wabbit” is a normal stop on the way to r. Keep the engine games silly and frequent, and let the tongue arrive on its own schedule; months of gentle practice are perfectly normal.

This lesson pairs with the Rabbit flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Sun — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Ss and its hiss with the sun card: your child traces the letter, rocks a toy snake to sleep with the world’s longest hiss, and lands the sound on a whole family of s-words.

What is this?

Ss is the letter that stands for the first sound in sun — teeth nearly closed, air hissing through, no voice: a sound that stretches as long as the breath does.

What does it mean?

S is the sound children already own: every "ssss" for quiet, every snake impression, every sparkler. This lesson just attaches the letter to a sound the mouth has practiced for years.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs the teeth-nearly-closed hiss, the long hold, and a sunshine of s-words: sun, sock, six, snake.

Why this matters

/s/ starts see, so, stop, sorry — words that steer a whole day. It is also the whisper twin of /z/, and the throat-check learned here keeps sun and zoo in their own letters.

What it teaches

Sustained air control (the longest sound in the set), teeth-to-tongue-channel shaping, and voice-off awareness with a familiar favourite.

Words to learn

ssunsocksixsnakesoap

Say this to your child

“"Make your teeth almost touch and hiss like a snake: ssss. That is s! S says ssss, like sun. Hiss it long: ssss… sun."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Ss. Teeth almost together, air hissing out — ssss! The sun sound."
  2. Finger-trace the Ss on the canvas — the curvy snake letter, drawn while hissing gently.
  3. Play the sleepy-snake game below; the hiss becomes a lullaby.
  4. Hiss three s-things: sun, sock, soap. Long hiss, short word.
  5. Finish with the hiss contest: the longest hiss picks the next s-word.

How to say it

Teeth nearly closed, tongue close behind them, air pushed through the gap, voice off: "ssss". It holds as long as breath allows — the set’s marathon sound.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Ss sits beside a smiling yellow sun with rounded rays, and the word "sun" is printed below — the morning friend that starts every sunny day with its sound.

Ask your child

"Is your throat quiet for s?" "How long can you hiss?" "What hisses in real life — a snake, a tyre, a sparkler?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "ssssun!" with a five-second hold, or organise the household hiss contest themselves — s brings out the competitor.

Out in the real world

Socks, soap, sandwiches and stairs; sun at wake-up, stars at bed-time. Snakes (real or toy) hiss on demand, and every "ssshh" for quiet is an s already in use.

Try it together

Sleepy-snake game: wrap a toy snake (or a scarf) in a blanket and rock it to sleep with the softest, longest hiss — "ssssss". But the moment the snake wakes, it must say an s-word before settling again: ssss-sock, ssss-sun, ssss-six. Rock, hiss, wake, word — until the snake finally sleeps for a full five-second hiss.

Understanding check

Ask for the sound and listen for the hold: a clean long hiss, throat silent. Then try z — same hiss, voice buzzing. If your child can switch the buzz on and off, both twins are handled.

Parent tips

If sun becomes "zun", the throat woke early — hand on the throat, restart the hiss. And use the hold as a game timer: hiss-length contests do the repetition for you.

This lesson pairs with the Sun flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Turtle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Tt and its quick tap with the turtle card: your child traces the letter, punches imaginary train tickets one t-word at a time, and feels the whisper-tap that never buzzes.

What is this?

Tt is the letter that stands for the first sound in turtle — a quick tongue tap just behind the top teeth with no voice: light, dry, over in a blink.

What does it mean?

T is d’s whisper twin: the same tap, the same spot, minus the buzz. Learning the pair by feel — tap with voice, tap without — is mouth-machinery knowledge for life.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs the quick dry tap, the silent throat, and a turtle-pace list of t-words: turtle, toe, tree, ten.

Why this matters

/t/ carries toe, tea, train and tick-tock — sounds a child hears from morning to night. It is also the most common ending tap in English (cat, sit, hot), so the tap learned here works at BOTH ends of words.

What it teaches

Tongue-tip speed, voice-off control (the d/t switch), and word-ending awareness — noticing that sounds can finish words too.

Words to learn

tturtletoetreetentick-tock

Say this to your child

“"Tap your tongue just behind your teeth — t! Quick and quiet, like a clock. T says t, like turtle. Tick-tock the sound: t, t, turtle."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Tt. Tap behind your teeth — quick and quiet: t! The turtle sound."
  2. Finger-trace the Tt on the canvas: one tall post and one roof, one tap per stroke.
  3. Play the train-ticket game below; every punch is a tap.
  4. Tap three t-things: turtle, toe, tea. Quick taps, slow words.
  5. Finish with the tick-tock finale: alternate t-t-t with d-d-d and feel the voice switch.

How to say it

Tongue tip taps the ridge behind the top teeth and releases, voice off: "t". One dry tap — no buzz, no puff-drag. The throat stays silent the whole time.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Tt sits beside a smiling green turtle, and the word "turtle" is printed below — the slowest animal in the set, perfect for the tap that is over fastest.

Ask your child

"Does your throat buzz for t?" "Where does your tongue tap?" "What t-word ticks?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "t-t-t-turtle!" like a careful little clock, or report the great discovery: "t and d are the same tap — one just whispers!"

Out in the real world

Tick-tock clocks, taps at the door, toast and tea; turtles at the pond, toes in the bath. The tap hides at the END of words too: cat, hot, sit — say them slowly and catch it.

Try it together

Train-ticket game: build a train from chairs. The conductor punches each passenger’s ticket — "t-t!" — and every ticket names a t-stop: Turtle Town, Tree Station, Ten Street. Choo-choo between stops, tap the tickets, announce the destinations. Late passengers must pay in t-words.

Understanding check

Ask for the sound and watch the throat: a dry tap with no buzz is the pass. Then alternate with d — same tap, buzzing. If your child can feel the switch, the twins are clocked and sorted.

Parent tips

If turtle comes out "durdle", the voice crept in — hand on the throat restarts the whisper. And try t at the END of words too: cat, hot, sit — the tap works both shifts.

This lesson pairs with the Turtle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Umbrella — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Uu and its relaxed "uh" with the umbrella card: your child traces the letter, plays the lazy game where doing nothing IS the sound, and meets the easiest vowel the mouth can make.

What is this?

Uu is the letter that stands for the first sound in umbrella — the short, loose “uh” that asks nothing of the mouth: no stretch, no rounding, no shape.

What does it mean?

U is the resting shape: the mouth’s default. After wide-open a, half-open e and tiny i, the mouth simply lets go — and that letting-go is the sound.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs the do-nothing mouth, a short "uh" (this is umbrella /u/, not unicorn /you/), and a puddle of u-words: up, under, us, umbrella.

Why this matters

/u/ runs up, under, us and uh-oh — the words of climbing, hiding and small disasters. It is also the last short vowel on the path; owning it completes the vowel family.

What it teaches

Muscle relaxation as a skill (the opposite of every other vowel), short-vowel discipline, and noticing the mouth’s resting position as a sound all by itself.

Words to learn

uumbrellaupunderusuh-oh

Say this to your child

“"Let everything go loose — no stretching, no rounding: uh. That is U’s sound, the umbrella one. Say it lazy: uh, uh, umbrella."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Uu. Let your mouth go loose — uh! The umbrella sound."
  2. Finger-trace the Uu on the canvas: one cup shape, drawn while the mouth hangs loose.
  3. Play the lazy-rest game below; the sound arrives when nothing tries.
  4. Say three u-things: up, under, umbrella. Mouth lazy, sound short.
  5. Finish with an uh-oh moment: drop a pretend cup — "uh-OH!" — and laugh.

How to say it

Mouth relaxed and barely open, tongue at rest, voice on: "uh". Nothing should feel stretched — if the lips round or spread, the vowel changed. Lazy is correct.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Uu sits beside a rainbow-striped umbrella, and the word "umbrella" is printed below — the brightest thing about a grey-rain sound.

Ask your child

"Is your mouth working hard or resting for uh?" "What do you say when you drop something?" "What goes up — and what goes under?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "uh-uh-umbrella!" with a proper shrug, or catch the sound mid-drama: "uh-oh! that starts with U!" — disaster and lesson in one.

Out in the real world

Up and under run the playground; uh-oh runs the kitchen. Umbrellas open on rain days, and every "uh-huh" and "uh-uh" in conversation is free practice.

Try it together

Lazy-rest game: slump into a big chair like the world’s tiredest lion. From the slump, say u-words with the least possible effort: up… under… us… umbrella. The rule: whoever tries the HARDEST loses; the laziest, loosest "uh" wins. Finish with a giant pretend yawn — the laziest u of all.

Understanding check

Show the card tomorrow and ask for the sound: a loose "uh" is the pass; a round "oo" or a stretchy "you" means long-u dropped by — restart lazy. Then hide the card and say umbrella slowly: the first sound should arrive without effort.

Parent tips

Short /u/ ("uh") and long /u/ ("you", as in unicorn) are different jobs — this card teaches the relaxed one. If umbrella drifts to "oo-mbrella", model three flat, lazy starts and let the shrug do the rest.

This lesson pairs with the Umbrella flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Van — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Vv and its buzz with the van card: your child traces the letter, plays an invisible violin through a v-word concert, and switches the voice ON — the difference between fan and van.

What is this?

Vv is the letter that stands for the first sound in van — top teeth on the bottom lip, air buzzing through WITH the voice on: vvv.

What does it mean?

V completes a famous pair: f whispers, v buzzes — same teeth, same lip, one switch. V is the first sound in the set taught entirely as a switch: find the f, turn the voice on.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs the teeth-on-lip shape WITH the throat buzzing, the f-to-v switch as a game, and a streetful of v-words: van, vet, violin, vase.

Why this matters

/v/ drives van, video, visit and five — wait, five hides v in the MIDDLE. That is v’s second secret: it loves word endings and middles (five, love, over) as much as beginnings.

What it teaches

Teeth-lip coordination with voicing, the on/off voice switch (f/v), and word-position awareness — v works at the front, middle and end.

Words to learn

vvanvetviolinvasefive

Say this to your child

“"Bite your lip softly like f — but turn your voice on: vvv. Feel it buzz? That is v! V says vvv, like van."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Vv. Teeth on the lip — but this time it BUZZES: vvv! The van sound."
  2. Finger-trace the Vv on the canvas: two slopes meeting in a point, one buzz down each slope.
  3. Play the violin game below — every bow stroke hums.
  4. Buzz three v-things: van, vase, violin. Feel the throat running.
  5. Finish with the f-v switch: fff…vvv…fff…vvv. The throat is the switch.

How to say it

Top teeth resting on the bottom lip, air through, voice ON: "vvv". It holds and hums. Same shape as f; the only difference is the buzzing throat.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Vv sits beside a white delivery van with a friendly face, and the word "van" is printed below — the vehicle that drives the buzz past your window most mornings.

Ask your child

"Is your throat buzzing or quiet for v?" "What is the difference between fan and van?" "What v-word drives?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "vvvvan!" with a full-buzz engine, or deliver the twin-fact unprompted: "f whispers, v buzzes — I can feel it in my neck!"

Out in the real world

Vans, vets and visits; violins at concerts, vases on shelves. Five and love carry v inside, and every video call starts with someone saying vee very clearly.
