Try it together

Violin game: prop an invisible violin under the chin, take an invisible bow, and play. Each bow stroke must hum a v-word: vvv-van, vvv-violin, vvv-five. Request songs by v-name, take turns as conductor and soloist, and end the concert with the longest vvv in the family’s history. Standing ovation optional; buzzing mandatory.

Understanding check

Ask for the sound and hold the throat: buzzing teeth-on-lip is the pass. Then run the switch test — fff (quiet) to vvv (buzz) and back. If your child can flip the switch, fan and van will never blur again.

Parent tips

If van arrives as fan, the voice is off — have your child hunt the buzz with a hand on their own throat, then flip between the two sounds until the switch feels like theirs. V wants the buzz; that is the whole letter.

This lesson pairs with the Van flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Whale — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Ww and its glide with the whale card: your child traces the letter, delivers a full weather report in w-words, and learns the sound that moves — lips round, then slide open.

What is this?

Ww is the letter that stands for the first sound in whale — lips rounded small, then gliding open into the vowel with the voice on: wuh.

What does it mean?

W is a moving sound: nothing stays still. The lips travel from a tight little "oo" shape out into the open word — a glide, not a stop. Sounds that move are actions as much as noises.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs the round-then-open glide, a running voice, and a seaful of w-words: whale, water, wave, wind.

Why this matters

/w/ powers water, want, we and wow — the splash words of childhood. It also looks like two v’s but sounds like nothing else, which makes it a favourite sorting puzzle.

What it teaches

Lip-glide control (round to open), voice carry-through, and connecting a physical motion to a sound — w is phonics choreography.

Words to learn

wwhalewaterwavewindwow

Say this to your child

“"Pucker up like you are going to say oo — then slide open: wuh. That is w! W says wuh, like whale. Glide it: w, w, whale."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Ww. Round your lips small, then open into the word — wuh! The whale sound."
  2. Finger-trace the Ww on the canvas: four waves, one glide each, voice running the whole way.
  3. Play the weather-reporter game below — the glide gets a whole forecast.
  4. Glide three w-things: whale, water, wave. Round, open, voice on.
  5. Finish with the arms-as-spout whoosh and one enormous WOW.

How to say it

Lips rounded tightly, then released open with the voice running: "wuh". The motion is one smooth glide — if the teeth touch the lip, it turned into v; keep teeth and lip apart.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Ww sits beside a blue whale spouting water, and the word "whale" is printed below — the spout itself is the sound’s shape: rounded, rising, opening out.

Ask your child

"Do your lips start round or open for w?" "Do they move or stay still?" "What w-word says itself in the bath?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "w-w-w-whale!" with rising arms, or report the news perfectly: "today is windy, wet and wavy" — a forecast with a phonics grade.

Out in the real world

Water play, windy walks and washing days are w-festivals. Waves at the beach (or in the bath), wobbly jelly, and every wow your child gasps — the glide is already in the day.

Try it together

Weather-reporter game: hand over a pretend microphone — your child is today’s weather reporter. The forecast must be w-heavy and delivered with glides: "today is windy! expect waves! whales everywhere! wow!" Swap roles and let the grown-up flub a report on purpose ("today is very… d-windy?") so the child can correct the news.

Understanding check

Ask for the sound and watch the lips: they should START rounded and MOVE open. If teeth bite the lip (vvvale), reset with "oo-uh" slid together fast. Then try r — w is round and gliding, r is curled and running.

Parent tips

If w bites into v, the teeth sneaked in — keep them behind the lip-line. The quick launch from a tiny lip-circle is the move to rehearse, and every weather report rehearses it for free.

This lesson pairs with the Whale flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Xylophone — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Xx, the alphabet’s famous oddball: mostly it says /ks/ at the END of words (box, fox, six), but on this card — at the start of xylophone — it borrows /z/. Both jobs are true, and children love the honesty.

What is this?

Xx has two jobs. Its day job is /ks/ at the end of words: box, fox, six, mix. Its rare gig is at the START of xylophone, where it sounds like /z/. This card shows the rare gig; the lesson teaches both, honestly.

What does it mean?

X teaches the most grown-up phonics truth: not every letter follows the rules, and THAT IS FINE. Meeting the exception as a friend — “this one is the weird one!” — builds reading confidence, not confusion. Out loud, twice, until it feels like insider knowledge.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs the /ks/ ending as x’s main job, the /z/ exception named out loud as special, and the pride of knowing the alphabet’s strangest letter.

Why this matters

/ks/ finishes box, fox, six and mix — words a child already counts with. And xylophone gives x a famous face, so the rarest letter never feels forgotten.

What it teaches

Ending-sound attention (most lessons hunt beginnings; x hunts endings), honest exception-handling, and the flexibility that keeps rules and quirks friends.

Words to learn

xxylophoneboxfoxsixmix

Say this to your child

“"X is a finisher — it loves the END of words: bo-ks! fo-ks! si-ks! Say them with me and listen to the ending. And xylophone? That is x’s one fancy day job, sounding like z."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Xx — the weird one! At the end of words it says ks: box! But here, at the start of xylophone, it borrows z."
  2. Finger-trace the Xx on the canvas: two crossing strokes — one for /k/, one for /s/, crossing like the sounds do.
  3. Play the treasure-box game below; every lid close clicks /ks/.
  4. End-say three x-words: box, fox, six. Listen for the sound at the END.
  5. Finish with one rainbow xylophone glissando and the honorary title: x-insider.

How to say it

/ks/ is two sounds in a row: the back click (/k/) straight into the hiss (/s/) — "ks", quick and dry, at word endings. For xylophone, borrow the buzzing /z/ — and say honestly that this one is the exception.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Xx sits beside a rainbow toy xylophone with two mallets, and the word "xylophone" is printed below — the most beautiful exception in the whole alphabet.

Ask your child

"Where does x like to hide — the start or the end of words?" "What does x say in box?" "And in xylophone? (Careful — it is the weird one!)"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "box ends with ks!" while slamming lids, or guard the secret jealously: "xylophone starts with a z-sound — I KNOW, it is weird."

Out in the real world

Boxes close with a /ks/ click all day: lunch boxes, toy boxes, shoe boxes. Foxes fill storybooks, six fills counting, and xylophones wait in every music corner.

Try it together

Treasure-box game: fill an imaginary box with treasure. Each item must be named and boxed away with a proper /ks/ click: a fo-ks! a bo-ks! si-ks gold coins! When the lid slams shut — "KS!" — the treasure is safe. Then, for the finale, play the xylophone: x’s one fancy, z-sounding day job, performed with two mallets and total seriousness.

Understanding check

Ask where x lives: "at the END — box, fox, six" is the pass, plus the bonus fact that xylophone is the famous weird one. Two jobs named out loud, both honest — x is fully understood.

Parent tips

Teach the exception AS an exception — children adore being told "this one is the weird one", and the honesty makes them phonics insiders. Never pretend xylophone starts with /ks/; they will catch you.

This lesson pairs with the Xylophone flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Yo-Yo — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Yy and its launching glide with the yo-yo card: your child traces the letter, yawns through a y-word game, and learns the sound that throws yes, you and yo-yo into the air.

What is this?

Yy is the letter that stands for the first sound in yo-yo — the tongue high and forward, gliding straight into the vowel like a launch: yuh.

What does it mean?

Y is a runway sound: it starts words the way a yo-yo leaves the hand — a quick slide that throws the word into the air. And y has a secret second life at word endings (happy, sky) saved for later.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs the quick glide off the tongue, the launch feel, and a handful of y-words: yo-yo, yes, you, yell.

Why this matters

/y/ launches yes, you, yawn and yummy — some of the most-used words in a small life. And the yawn game makes it the only letter sound a child can practice while genuinely falling asleep.

What it teaches

Front-glide control (the same runway as the vowels that follow), quick launch-and-release, and the social magic of yes and thank-you practice built in.

Words to learn

yyo-yoyesyouyellyummy

Say this to your child

“"Slide your tongue up and let the word jump off: yuh. That is y! Y says yuh, like yo-yo. Launch it: y, y, yo-yo."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Yy. The tongue slides and launches the word — yuh! The yo-yo sound."
  2. Finger-trace the Yy on the canvas: one long arm and one short — the shape of a hand throwing a yo-yo down and catching it.
  3. Play the yawny game below; the glide arrives with the yawns.
  4. Launch three y-things: yo-yo, yes, yummy. One glide each, thrown into the room.
  5. Finish with a fist-up-fist-down yo-yo trick — yo, yo — and a real catch.

How to say it

Tongue high and forward, then a quick glide into the vowel with the voice on: "yuh". One launch, no hold — y never waits, it throws.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Yy sits beside a blue yo-yo with a star and a long string, and the word "yo-yo" is printed below — the only toy whose name says itself twice, one y per syllable.

Ask your child

"Does y stay still or launch the word?" "What is the politest y-word?" "Can you say yo-yo without laughing?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "y-y-yo-yo!" with matching fist pumps, or use the lesson politically: "yes starts with y — I said the y-word!"

Out in the real world

Yo-yos, yoghurt and yawns; yellow things, yachts in books, and every yes and thank-you exchange of the day. The glide launches manners as often as toys.

Try it together

Yawny game: y is the letter of yawns — so yawn. Each giant pretend yawn must land on a y-word: yaaaawn… yo-yo! yaaaawn… yes! yaaaawn… yummy! The bigger the yawn, the further the word flies. Bedtime bonus: this is the only phonics game that ends in an actual nap.

Understanding check

Ask for the sound: a quick gliding "yuh" is the pass. Then say yo-yo syllable by syllable — two yaws, two y-sounds, one word. If the glide launches cleanly, y’s first job is owned (the vowel job at word endings waits happily for later).

Parent tips

If y comes out heavy as "juh", lighten it — the tongue slides, it does not jump (that is j’s move). The oo-yes trick helps: say "ee" then open fast — ee-yes becomes yes, and the glide is discovered.

This lesson pairs with the Yo-Yo flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · PHONICS & BEGINNING SOUNDS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Zebra — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches Zz, the last letter on the path: the s-hiss with the voice switched on. Your child traces the letter, zips through a z-word parade, and closes the whole alphabet with the loudest coat in the set.

What is this?

Zz is the letter that stands for the first sound in zebra — the snake hiss of s with the voice buzzing: zzz. Same teeth, same tongue, one switch turned on.

What does it mean?

Z is the alphabet’s finish line, learned as a switch: find the hiss, turn on the buzz. Children who just learned s can borrow its whole mouth-shape — z is s wearing a bee costume.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs the buzzing hiss, the s-to-z switch as a party trick, and a parade of z-words: zebra, zoo, zip, zero.

Why this matters

/z/ carries zip, zoo, zoom and zero — the words of speed and nothing. It closes the alphabet with a built-in celebration: the sound-wall finale, where all twenty-six sounds line up for one last parade.

What it teaches

Voice-switch mastery (the s/z pair completes the twin collection), buzz control on a familiar shape, and the memory-and-recall feat of the A–Z sound wall.

Words to learn

zzebrazoozipzerozoom

Say this to your child

“"Hiss like a snake — now turn your voice on and feel it buzz: zzz. That is z! Z says zzz, like zebra. The last letter, with the loudest coat."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Zz. Hiss like s — but buzz! zzz. The zebra sound, and the LAST letter!"
  2. Finger-trace the Zz on the canvas: across, diagonal, across — one buzz per stroke.
  3. Play the zip-up game below; the sound lives in every jacket.
  4. Buzz three z-things: zebra, zoo, zip. Sss with the switch on.
  5. Finish with the sound-wall finale: all the letter sounds from A to Z, ending on the loudest zebra cheer.

How to say it

Teeth nearly closed like s, air through, voice ON: "zzz". It hums while it hisses. If z comes out as s, the throat went quiet — hand on the throat, switch the bee back on.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the big navy pair Zz sits beside a black-and-white striped zebra, and the word "zebra" is printed below — the alphabet’s boldest coat, on the very last letter of the path.

Ask your child

"Is z buzzing or quiet?" "What is the difference between sun and zoo?" "What z-word zips?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "zzz-zebra!" like a bee landing, or announce the graduation moment: "I did the WHOLE alphabet — A to zzz!"

Out in the real world

Zips on jackets, bags and tents buzz all day. Zoo trips, zooming cars and zero biscuits left close the set’s vocabulary — and bedtime bees provide the buzz on demand.

Try it together

Zip-up game: hand over a real jacket (or mime one). Zip it slowly while buzzing — "zzz-zz-zz-IP!" — and each successful zip earns a z-word: zip, zoo, zebra, zero. Unzip, buzz backwards, zip again. Then the finale: the whole alphabet’s sounds, paraded from A to Z — the zebra always closes the show and always gets the biggest cheer.

Understanding check

Ask for the sound and listen for the buzz inside the hiss. Then the grand test: sun (quiet hiss) and zoo (buzzing hiss) back to back — if your child can switch the voice on and off, the twin collection is complete, and so is the alphabet.

Parent tips

Many children say z like s at first — the mouth shape is right, the switch is just off. Hand on the throat, buzz it on, and end every session with the A–Z sound wall: nothing finishes the alphabet like the zebra’s cheer.

This lesson pairs with the Zebra flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28).
